chapters.title: Chapter 2: The New Multipolar World: US, China, and the Rest

lessons.title: China Plus One: Supply Chain Realignment and What It Means for Indian Manufacturing

body.text: China Plus One is not a company deciding to leave China. It is a company deciding it can no longer afford to have every critical supplier in one country, and India is one of a handful of places competing hard to be the plus one.

children.text: The previous lesson covered tariffs and export controls as the sharp end of the US-China rivalry. This lesson covers its slower, quieter consequence: global manufacturers deliberately rebuilding supply chains to reduce how much of their production sits inside one country. This shift, commonly called China Plus One, is one of the few geopolitical trends that shows up as a genuine multi-year tailwind for parts of the Indian economy, rather than purely as a risk to manage.
What China Plus One Actually Means

China Plus One does not mean abandoning China, which remains the world's largest and most efficient manufacturing base for a huge range of goods. It means a company deliberately adding a second production location for at least part of its supply chain, so that a single country's tariffs, export controls, lockdowns, or political tensions cannot shut down its entire operation at once. It is a diversification strategy for companies, built on exactly the same logic an investor uses when diversifying a portfolio, do not hold all your risk in one place.
Why Now: Three Forces Driving the Shift

cells: Tariffs and export controls, covered in the previous lesson, made a China-only supply chain a direct tariff and compliance risk for companies selling into the US market
Extended factory shutdowns in China during 2020-2022 exposed how much of global manufacturing, from electronics to basic medicines, sat concentrated in one country
Wages and land costs in China's manufacturing hubs have risen steadily over the past decade, narrowing China's cost advantage over alternative locations for labour-intensive production

children.text: The Countries Competing for This Shift
India is not the only country chasing this opportunity, and it is worth being honest about where it currently stands relative to its main competitors.

body.title: India vs Vietnam vs Mexico, as China Plus One Destinations

columns.label: India's strengths
points: Large domestic market, so factories can serve local demand and exports together
A large, low-cost, and increasingly skilled labour pool
Strong government incentives through schemes like Production Linked Incentive, or PLI

columns.label: What Vietnam and Mexico do better
points: Vietnam has smaller scale but faster, more established electronics assembly ecosystems already integrated with China's supply chains
Mexico offers proximity to the US market and USMCA trade preferences, ideal for companies specifically diversifying away from China for US-bound goods
Both generally rank ahead of India on ease of doing business and logistics infrastructure metrics, though India has been closing this gap

children.text: India's Pitch: PLI, Make in India, and the Assembly Boom

The Indian government's main tool here is the Production Linked Incentive, or PLI, scheme, which offers direct cash incentives to companies for incremental manufacturing and sales in India, across sectors including electronics, pharmaceuticals, and specialty chemicals. The clearest visible result so far is in smartphone assembly, where Apple's India-based assemblers, including Foxconn and Tata Electronics, have scaled up rapidly.

stats.label: India's share of global iPhone production
stats.context: Up from a low single-digit share only a few years earlier, according to widely reported industry estimates

stats.label: Total PLI outlay announced
stats.context: Across 14 sectors since the scheme's 2020 launch, with electronics as one of the largest individual allocations

stats.label: Electronics exports
stats.context: Driven heavily by smartphone assembly, though India still imports many of the higher-value components used inside those phones

children.text: The Catch: Assembly Is Not the Same as a Supply Chain

This is the nuance that gets lost in the excitement: a phone assembled in India is not the same as a phone manufactured end-to-end in India. Many high-value components, chips, displays, and specialised parts, are still imported, often from China itself, and simply put together in Indian factories. This makes India's China Plus One story real but partial. It is genuine progress on final assembly and jobs, but it does not yet mean India has replicated China's deep, component-level manufacturing base. Semiconductor ambitions illustrate this well, a proposed joint venture between Vedanta and Foxconn to build a chip fabrication plant in Gujarat fell apart in 2023 after delays, with Vedanta subsequently pursuing the project with new partners, a reminder that this structural shift is real but not frictionless or guaranteed to play out on the original timeline.

body.text: The most useful investor lens here is not 'is India benefiting from China Plus One', which is broadly true, but 'how far up the value chain is this specific company or sector moving', since final assembly, component manufacturing, and design each carry very different margins and durability.

body.title: Assembly vs Manufacturing
body.scenario: A friend tells you India has 'basically replaced China' in electronics manufacturing, pointing to rising smartphone export numbers as proof.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's distinction between assembly and manufacturing, how would you respond?
body.modelAnswer: Rising smartphone exports are real and meaningful, but they mostly reflect growth in final assembly, phones being put together in India, rather than full, component-level manufacturing. Many high-value inputs, such as chips and displays, are still imported, often from China. India has made genuine progress in China Plus One, but 'replacing China' would require moving much further up the value chain into component manufacturing and design, which is a longer and less certain journey than the assembly numbers alone suggest.

body.title: What Does China Plus One Actually Require?
body.question: Which of the following best describes the China Plus One strategy?
options: Companies completely exiting China and relocating all production elsewhere
Companies adding at least one additional production location alongside their existing China operations, to reduce concentration risk
A government policy that bans companies from manufacturing in China
A trade agreement between China and a second country
body.explanation: China Plus One is a diversification strategy where companies add a second manufacturing location rather than fully exiting China, which remains central to global manufacturing. The goal is reducing concentration risk, not eliminating China exposure entirely.

cards.definition: A corporate strategy of adding at least one additional manufacturing location alongside existing China-based operations, to reduce the risk of overconcentration in a single country.

An Indian government scheme offering direct cash incentives to companies for incremental manufacturing output and sales achieved in India, across sectors including electronics, pharmaceuticals, and specialty chemicals.
Relocating supply chains to a country geographically close to the end market, such as companies moving production to Mexico to serve the US market more efficiently.

The full sequence of activities, from raw materials and component manufacturing through design, assembly, and final sale, that goes into a finished product. Different stages carry very different profit margins.

points: China Plus One is companies diversifying part of their supply chain to a second country, not abandoning China, which remains central to global manufacturing
Three forces are driving the shift: the US-China rivalry's tariffs and export controls, the supply shocks exposed by COVID-19, and rising costs within China itself

India competes with Vietnam and Mexico for this opportunity, each with different strengths; India leads on scale and domestic market size but still trails on ease of doing business and logistics infrastructure

India's PLI scheme has driven a genuine boom in smartphone assembly and electronics exports, but assembly is not the same as full component-level manufacturing, many high-value inputs are still imported

The shift is real but not frictionless, as shown by the 2023 collapse of the original Vedanta-Foxconn chip fabrication joint venture, and investors should track how far up the value chain a company is actually moving, not just headline export or output growth

This lesson references specific companies and government schemes for educational, factual illustration only, and is not a recommendation to invest in any company or sector named here.
